In the VotingEscrow system, delegators can delegate their locked voting power to another address. However, the contract design allows accounts that are on the blocklist to immediately undelegate after calling forceUndelegate(), and this process resets locked_.end to the current account's lock expiration time. Malicious users can exploit this by controlling the relationship between the delegator and the delegatee, intentionally triggering self-blocking when they want to unlock early, thus forcing the undelegation and bypassing the original commitment restrictions that should last until the end of the locking period. This allows them to redeem tokens early and repeat the process.
The current implementation of the VotingEscrow contract doesn’t support fee on transfer tokens

Blocklist.block() checks if an address is a contract before blocking it by only using _isContract(addr), which relies on confirming that extcodesize > 0. This determination depends on the current code length of the address. Malicious actors can call selfdestruct() after interacting with the system to delete the contract, causing extcodesize to become 0 and bypassing the check. They could even use CREATE2 to redeploy the same or different logic contract at the same address to continue interaction.

There is no check to determine if the caller's lock has expired. As a result, users with expired locks can delegate to other active locks as long as the locked amount has not been withdrawn. This can be used to influence voting power.

In VotingEscrow.increaseUnlockTime(), when constructing the oldLocked struct passed to _checkpoint(), the oldLocked.end is erroneously set to the new lock's unlock_time instead of the original oldUnlockTime.
Unsafe casting from int128 can cause wrong accounting of locked amounts
_checkpoint update is missed incase locked_.delegatee |= msg.sender

When a user is added to the Blocklist, they can avoid having their funds stuck by calling forceUndelegate() (triggered during blocking) to revoke their delegation. However, if the system administrator changes the blocklist contract address during a migration or due to an error, and the new contract returns true for isBlocked() for a specific account that has not gone through the normal blocking process (and thus has not triggered forceUndelegate()), that account will be treated as blocked.Consequently, the user's tokens become locked in the contract, as there is no mechanism for lifting the block or recovering funds.

An attacker can use a flashloan and the quitLock function to achieve a large amount of votes for one transaction. It can, depends on the implementation of the modules that will use this contract, be used to pass malicious proposals or exploit any feature that depends on the voting balance.

If an active proposal accumulates over 80% of total votes but fails to execute, the remaining votes are insufficient to activate a new proposal due to the 20% endorsement threshold, effectively locking governance indefinitely and preventing vote reclamation or further proposals.

When all contracts have been deployed and/or initialized, the OlympusVotes contract does not mint an initial token supply. This would allow users to be able to submit proposals, then vote and execute proposals if there has been no token supply (totalSupply = 0).

An attacker can front-run a reduction in token withdrawal approval by executing a withdrawal using the higher previous allowance, and then withdraw again under the newly reduced approval, resulting in over-withdrawal beyond the intended limit.

The Operator::setReserveFactor function updates the reserveFactor but fails to trigger the necessary regeneration logic. The Range module may operate with outdated capacity thresholds, potentially leaving the bond market open or closed incorrectly.

In getloan() and replayloan(),the safetransfer and safetransferfrom doesn't check the existence of code at the token address. If safetransfer() and safetransferfrom() are called on a token address that doesn't have contract in it, it will always return success, bypassing the return value check.

If the asset price remains outside the defined wall price for longer than _config.regenWait, RBS may automatically redeploy funds even though the price has not returned to the safe zone. This could result in the treasury buying or selling at prices far from the market value, causing loss of funds.

The executeProposal() function resets the activeProposal state before executing the proposal instructions. An attacker can repeatedly re-enter and execute the same instructions through nested calls, potentially leading to unauthorized module installations or fund manipulation.
The method Governance.submitProposal doesn't check if the proposalId (stored in a different contract) exists already as a valid proposal in getProposalMetadata.

subtag: Bad Condition, Does not match with Doc
description: When the voting tokens are transferrable, one user can first use her or his votes to call the following endorseProposal function to endorse a proposal and then transfer these votes to another user. The other user can use these votes to endorse the same proposal again afterwards. Because of the double-endorsement, the (totalEndorsementsForProposal[proposalId_] * 100) < VOTES.totalSupply() * ENDORSEMENT_THRESHOLD condition can become true so the proposal can be activated by calling the activateProposal function below.
Endorsed votes by a user do not decrease after the user's votes are revoked

subtag: Implementation Error, Price Manipulation / Arbitrage opportunity
description: A TWAP is a Time-Weighted average price, but the algorithm below does not take into account the time between observations

The activateProposal() function allows immediate replacement of the active proposal without any delay. Since the vote() function does not specify a proposal ID, users might unknowingly vote on a different proposal if activateProposal() is called right before or in the same block, creating potential for front-running and governance manipulation.

Once a user votes on a proposal, they cannot vote again—even if new votes are issued or revoked during the voting period. This creates inconsistencies between the recorded vote and the evolving total supply, potentially distorting quorum and outcome calculations, and undermining the reliability of governance results.

A user can call vote() and then immediately reclaim their voting tokens using reclaimVotes() within the same transaction. This temporarily hides their voting power from the voter_admin, preventing any revocation via revokeVotesFrom() .

The TreasuryCustodian.revokePolicyApprovals() function can be abused to revoke withdrawal approvals from EOAs. Since the function only checks isActive() and interprets a failed call as false, any EOA (which naturally returns false when isActive() is called) can have its approvals griefed.

There are no checks to ascertain that the policy being removed is registered in the Kernel. Trying to remove a non-registered results in the policy registered at 0th index of activePolicies being removed.
A malicious user holding just enough voting power to meet the ENDORSEMENT_THRESHOLD (e.g., 20%) can repeatedly submit and activate dummy proposals.
If all reward tokens are withdrawn using withdrawUnspentRewards(), the internal _issueReward() function will fail on the next beat() call due to insufficient token balance.

In both RANGE.sol and Operator.sol, the constructor() functions accept parameters like spreads and factors, but fail to enforce the same input validation checks found in the corresponding setter functions such as setSpreads(), setThresholdFactor(), and setCushionFactor().
The voter_admin role can mint unlimited VOTES, and since there's no cap on totalSupply, this allows the admin to arbitrarily adjust the execution threshold by inflating the supply.

In getCurrentPrice(), the staleness check for OHM price data allows a freshness window of 3 * observationFrequency, whereas the reserve token price uses a stricter 1 * observationFrequency. This inconsistency can cause the entire price-fetching logic to revert if the reserve token’s oracle doesn't update as frequently as expected, even when the OHM oracle is within the acceptable window.

The repayLoan() function in OlympusTreasury measures the received repayment amount by comparing token balances before and after safeTransferFrom(). However, if the token is an ERC777 with a tokensToSend() hook, an attacker can perform a reentrant call to Operator::swap() within that hook. This alters the Treasury's token balance mid-execution, tricking the contract into overestimating how much debt was repaid.

If wallSpread is set to 10000 (100%), the lower wall price computed in RANGE::updatePrices() becomes zero. This causes a division by zero in Operator::_activate() when computing invWallPrice. When the market enters a state where the lower wall is active and the price falls between the cushion and wall levels, operate() will revert.

After a loan is issued from the Treasury via getLoan(), the getReserveBalance() function still reports an inflated token balance that includes the borrowed tokens and it breaks other contract functionality like swaps.

The repayLoan() function in the Treasury module calculates the repaid amount by comparing the Treasury’s token balance before and after safeTransferFrom(). If a malicious actor can exploit a cross-contract hook (e.g., protocol revenue payout or ERC777 tokensToSend behavior) during the transfer call to send additional tokens to the Treasury, the contract mistakenly attributes those tokens as loan repayment, reducing the attacker's debt unfairly.
Function OlympusPrice.getCurrentPrice retrieves price using latestRoundData but the implementation is missing essential security checks which can result in stale and incorrect prices being returned.
The precision is lost in moving average calculations as the difference is calculated separately and added each time, while it typically can be small enough to lose precision in the division involved.

If Actions.MigrateKernel is not placed as the last instruction in a proposal, subsequent instructions—such as DeactivatePolicy—will fail due to the Kernel reference having changed mid-execution. Since affected functions rely on onlyKernel checks, they will revert, rendering the proposal unexecutable.

In Kernel._activatePolicy, no checks are done to ensure that the policy is not already registered in the Kernel contract. The check policy_.isActive() depends on an external call, and should be less preferred over contract's storage in this case. Successfully adding duplicate policy would result in failure when trying to deactivate it.

In both withdrawReserves() and in getLoan(), _checkApproval() is used to verify user has enough approval and subtracts the withdraw / loan amount. Therefore, there is no differentiation in validation between loan approval and withdraw approval.

subtag: Implementation Error, Price Manipulation / Arbitrage opportunity
description: If Heart::beat() has not been called for a while, a user can invoke it multiple times within a single block, collecting the reward repeatedly and triggering redundant logic executions, which can lead to unnecessary updates and excessive token payouts.

subtag: Price Manipulation / Arbitrage opportunity, Stale Value
description: Even when the beat() function is no longer called and oracle data becomes stale, the protocol continues to allow swaps against the RBS walls and cushion bonds. This enables arbitrage traders to exploit outdated prices, potentially draining treasury assets through favorable zero-slippage trades.

After deployment, the admin address in the Kernel contract can only be changed to another contract, not to an EOA. Since only contracts like INSTR can call executeAction, and INSTR restricts targets to contracts, it's impossible to later assign admin rights to an EOA, which may have been the intended governance executor.

_afterTokenTransfer incorrectly transfers voting units between "user addresses" instead of "delegated addresses," causing an underflow in the unchecked block of _moveDelegates that grants accounts maximum voting power.

_afterTokenTransfer incorrectly attempts to subtract voting units from the "token owner" instead of their "delegate," causing a revert when the owner’s direct voting balance is zero after delegation, thereby freezing NFT transfers and burns.

_writeCheckpoint fails to consolidate multiple updates within the same block, allowing multiple checkpoints with identical timestamps to corrupt the binary search in getPastVotes, leading to incorrect voting weight calculations.

_delegate directly accesses the delegation mapping instead of using a helper function to resolve the default delegate, causing the initial prevDelegate to be address(0) and allowing users to mint "new" votes to themselves during their first self-delegation.

The implementation failed to follow OpenZeppelin ERC721Votes’ documentation: “Tokens do not count as votes until they are delegated.” The _transferFrom() function does not move delegated votes from the source’s delegates to the destination’s delegates; instead, it directly moves votes from the source to the destination.This allows users to create new accounts and repeatedly delegate to indefinitely increase their voting power, holding more votes than they actually should.

At the early stage of the deployed DAO, if the token supply is low, the calculation settings.token.totalSupply() * settings.quorumThresholdBps) / 10_000 inside function quorum() may return 0, causing proposal.quorumVotes to be set to 0.

The unpause() function incorrectly assumes auction.tokenId == 0 always implies the first auction hasn't started, causing it to re-initialize a new auction and reset the state, which orphans the existing bid and NFT #0 if the first auction was already active.

In the Token.mint() function, a while loop checks _isForFounder(tokenId), and inside _isForFounder, _tokenId is taken modulo 100 before querying tokenRecipient. If the first 100 tokenIds' tokenRecipient entries are all vesting (such as when the total founders’shares sums to 100%, filling all entries), _isForFounder will always return true, causing mint() to enter an infinite loop.

Due to the incorrect modulo operation when filling the tokenRecipient mapping, some founders may receive IDs greater than 100, resulting in those IDs never being minted.Under certain allocation settings ((100 / pct1) - (100 / pct2) == 1), founders will receive fewer tokens than their configured percentage.

The cancel function uses a strict "greater than" check ($>$) for the proposal threshold, whereas the propose function allows equality ($\ge$), enabling anyone to cancel a proposal if the proposer's voting power exactly equals the threshold.
Absence of reasonable maximum and minimum bounds for critical parameters in governance, treasury, and auction.

_delegate allows users to delegate to address(0), which clears the owner’s voting checkpoints without updating their delegation status; consequently, _afterTokenTransfer later attempts to subtract votes from the now-zero balance, causing a revert that permanently bricks token transfers and burning.

When a user delegates voting power to address(0) through _delegate() , _to's vote weight won’t change since _writeCheckpoint() (where the acutal vote weight changes) inside _moveDelegateVotes() wil be skipped (because _to is address(0)).The delegation of voting power to the address(0) will permanently burn that voting power.

subtag: Does not match with Doc, Invalid Validation, Missing Upper/Lower Bound Check
description: MetadataRenderer uses a fixed-size array of 16 for tokenAttributes but allows owners to add more than 15 properties, causing an "Index out of bounds" revert during the onMinted callback and permanently bricking the token minting process.

The protocol use token.totalSupply() to calculates quorumVotes, but token.totalSupply() takes into account burned tokens and tokens held in the auction contract, which don’t have any actual voting power, which means the actual quorumThresholdBps is equal or higher than the setted quorumThresholdBps.
 The worst-case scenario is that quorum becomes so high that a proposal cannot pass even if everybody voted and everybody voted for, potentially locking funds into the contract.

Lack of address(0) check for vetoer address in initialize() and 2 step address changing process (set pending address and claim by himself) in updateVetoer() for vetoer address, resulting in veteor address be set to address(0) or an arbitrary address.

_createAuction() wraps the token.mint() call in a try-catch block, however, due to the Error(string memory) behind catch, this will only catch reverts that comes from the require keyword and not the reverts with custom errors or other kinds of errors (arithmetic over/underflow etc.).In case of an error at mint() the auction won’t be settled till the owner and pauses the contract.

The veto function grants the vetoer absolute, permanent, and unrestricted power to block any proposal regardless of its state or community consensus, creating a single point of failure where a compromised or malicious actor can indefinitely paralyze the DAO's governance.

The proposalId is derived solely from proposal content without incorporating the msg.sender or a nonce. This allows an attacker to front-run a legitimate proposal, create it first, and immediately cancel it, permanently preventing the original content from being proposed again due to the PROPOSAL_EXISTS check.

The _createAuction function uses a try/catch block for token.mint(), which can be manipulated via EIP-150’s 63/64 gas rule. By providing a specific amount of gas, an attacker can force the minting call to fail due to Out-of-Gas while leaving enough gas for the catch block to execute _pause(), effectively allowing any user to halt the auction.

Auction parameter setters (e.g., duration, reserve price) lack state checks or caching mechanisms, allowing owners to modify critical settings during an active auction, which can lead to immediate settlement, failed bids, or manipulated user expectations.

At the early stage of a DAO, inside function proposalThreshold() it is possible that proposalThreshold rounds down to 0 because the token supply is low, causing the check in propose() not revert, so anyone can create proposals. Besides this, quorum() will return 0 due to the same logic, resulting in the proposal to be executed without being votes.
Impact: Anyone can create a proposal and the proposal can pass without anyone votes.

With collections of more than 20000 NFTs, proposalThreshold() and quorum() can’t return 1 since the lowest number of settings.proposalThresholdBps and settings.quorumThresholdBps are 1 and the divisor is set to 10000.High total supply NFT can have threshold set to 1.

In the Governor contract, parameters related to proposal (e.g., quorum & threshold) are depends on the total supply in the current timestamp but not the previous timestamp, so these values can be changed if total supply cahnges later in the same block because tehy are still eligible to vote.Attckers can lower the threshold and quorum by incresaing totalSupply.

The protocol accepts both externally owned accounts (EOAs) and contract accounts as users, without restricting users to only EOAs. Users can transfer their voting power to a smart contract that offers higher incentives, resulting in that contract having increased voting power.

The initialize function performs an unsafe cast of founderPct to uint8 when calculating the cumulative totalOwnership. If a founder's percentage is a multiple of 256 (e.g., 256, 512), the truncated value becomes 0, bypassing the "maximum 100%" check and allowing malicious founders to monopolize the base token distribution logic.

The burn function in the Token contract does not decrement settings.totalSupply. Since founder allocations are based on a fixed schedule relative to a continuously increasing counter, burning unsold auction tokens reduces the actual circulating supply without adjusting the founders' fixed claim, effectively granting them a higher ownership percentage than the intended fixed percentage.

Governor.transferOwnership() and Auction.transferOwnership() can be called by Treasury.sol through a governance proposal, causing a mismatch between the contract owner and settings.treasury.settings.treasury is not able to modify any governance parameters.

The "greedy" founder minting logic processes all reserved slots consecutively in a single mint() call. If the vestExpiry (vesting expiration) occurs mid-cycle, a founder with a higher reserved index range may capture nearly their entire 100-token-cycle allocation, while other founders lose their scheduled tokens for that cycle entirely.
It is not possible to mint a ERC721 token if its properties has different length than it's items.

addProperties() doesn’t check newly added property has at least one item. Minting becomes impossible if  a property without items was added, and an item is only possible through a new governance proposal to be added to a property.

MetadataRenderer.onMinted() allows minting tokens without verifying that properties have been set, leading to tokens with no attributes. Such tokens won’t be able to render since MetaRenderer.getAttributes will revert with TOKEN_NOT_MINTED error.

In Governor.state(), 
the logic for determining whether a proposal is defeated uses the < operator but not <=. When forVotes and againstVotes are equal, the proposal is not considered defeated even if forVotes does not exceed againstVotes. Proposals can passed without majority support.

If the governor key is leaked, an attacker can frontrun the execution with a malicious _calldata after the notice period, bypassing the intended upgrade protection. Without early detection of key leakage, the system cannot prevent malicious upgrades.
The BLOCK_PERIOD is incorrectly set to 13 seconds instead of Ethereum's actual 12-second PoS block time, causing priority transactions to expire 5.5 hours earlier than expected on zkSync.
AutoPxGlp and AutoPxGmx are not compliant with ERC4626 standard, previewWithdraw should round up.

The Vault's first deposit lacks a minimum amount or fixed shares mechanism, allowing the first depositor to use a very small number of shares to increase the share price after additional assets are transferred in. By using the rounding down formula, subsequent depositors may receive very few shares, ultimately allowing the first depositor to siphon off the principal from other depositors.

invariant() performs division before multiplication when executing FullMath.mulDiv(), leading to data being truncated when dealing with low-precision decimal tokens. This allows attackers to extract assets while still satisfying the invariant condition.

mint() uses the input parameter collateral to determine the actual amount received, overlooking the fact that fee-on-transfer ERC20 tokens can lead to a shortage of collateral. This results in a failed check and prevents support for such tokens.

When adding liquidity for the first time, the protocol requires users to manually input amount0Min, amount1Min, and liquidity simultaneously, lacking on-chain verification or automatic calculation mechanisms. This can result in imprecise values and may lead to reverts.

The design of upperBound in relation to liquidity distribution can create incentives for liquidity concentration and front-running liquidations as market prices and borrowing behaviors change. This allows the fastest participants to exit early or lock in funds to capture MEV (Maximal Extractable Value) profits.
zeroswap/UniswapV2Library.sol Wrong init code hash in UniswapV2Library.pairFor() will break UniswapV2Oracle, UniswapV2Router02, SushiRoll

The method checks the amount received from the user with the condition if (balanceAfter < balanceBefore + collateral) revert InsufficientInputError();. However, the user may actually pay more collateral. In this case, no funds are returned to the caller, and they do not receive additional liquidity or shares.
Division before multiplication incurs unnecessary precision loss

In the rebalance() function of Timeswap V2, when a user executes TimeswapV2PoolRebalance.GivenLong1, the contract mistakenly uses pool.long0Balance as the calculation parameter, whereas it should be pool.long1Balance.
In ERC1155, using totalSupply() + 1 as the new tokenId may lead to duplication, which can result in incorrect asset allocation.

The collect() function calls transferFees() before long0Fees, long1Fees, and shortFees are properly initialized. As a result, the actual transfer amount is zero. Although the fees in _feesPositions are still burned, the user does not receive any funds, leading to asset loss and state inconsistency.

The ERC1155Enumerable contract does not correctly update _currentIndex, _allTokens, and _allTokensIndex during token minting and burning. As a result, even when a token ID's supply drops to zero, its associated indices are retained, causing totalSupply() to return inaccurate results.

_removeTokenFromAllTokensEnumeration can never be called, because of wrong order of if statement and _idTotalSupply[id] -= amount;. This leads to totalSupply do not correctly minus 1 when all token amounts for a specific tokenId get burned.

subtag: Does not match with Doc, Fee On Transfer Token
description: whitelisting token0 and token1 ensuring no fee-on-transfer token is allowed when deploying a new Timeswap V2 Option pair contract
Due to the wrong calculation of short and long tokens during the leverage and deleverage process, the users can suffer financial loss while the protocol will lose fees

The vulnerability in the add512 function arises from an incomplete overflow check. It only checks whether addendA1 > sum1, but fails to account for the case when addendA1 == sum1 and an overflow occurs in the lower 256 bits (sum0).
_ownedTokensIndex is SHARED by different owners, as a result, _removeTokenFromAllTokensEnumeration() might remove the wrong tokenId.

When an LP calls mint, the contract updates global fee growth (short, long0, long1) but fails to update the LP’s LiquidityPosition. This leads to a mismatch between the user's position and global state, potentially causing the LP to receive fewer fees.
Calling MsgValueSimulator with non-zero msg.value triggers a self-call that bypasses onlySelf checks and may lead to unexpected behavior or stuck funds.

Calling forceDeployOnAddress() without callConstructor sets the contract to constructing state permanently, making it behave like an EOA and preventing any function calls. This can silently break protocol logic and disable critical contracts.
User transactions with non-zero ETH can trigger system contracts via rawCall, bypassing the intended isSystem restrictions and potentially enabling dangerous behavior.
The fallback() function in DefaultAccount lacks payable, causing ETH transfers with unrecognized calldata to fail, breaking EVM compatibility and affecting protocol interoperability.
Failed force deployments can trap ETH in the ContractDeployer contract, making the funds unrecoverable and unusable for future deployments.

The moveLiquidity() function unconditionally removes the fromIndex from positionIndexes, even when only a partial LP amount was successfully moved. This causes the remaining LP to become inaccessible and frozen, leading to permanent fund lockup.

The moveLiquidity function incorrectly sets toPosition.depositTime to the source bucket's deposit time, which may be stale and not reflect the actual deposit state in the destination bucket. If the destination bucket has gone bankrupt after that time, the moved LPs will be considered defaulted and permanently inaccessible, resulting in irreversible fund loss.

Anyone can attach insignificant liquidity positions to another user's Position NFT without permission, bloating the positionIndexes array. This can lead to DOS during reward calculations due to exceeding the gas limit and also prevent the NFT from being burned, locking the owner’s assets.

subtag: Does not match with Doc, Precision Loss
description: In Ajna Grants, the 10% reward allocated to delegating voters is actually spent, but not accounted for when updating the treasury after a funding round. This causes the contract to double-count the 10% delegation rewards, leading to inaccurate treasury values and potential long-term precision errors or underfunded distributions.
In Ajna’s RewardsManager, an incorrect calculation of updatedRewards_ occurs when rewardsClaimedInEpoch already exceeds the pool’s rewardsCap, causing an underflow during subtraction.

In PositionManager.memorializePositions, if a bucket is found bankrupt after a prior deposit, the system zeroes out the lender’s previously tracked LP balance — even if there are still unclaimed rewards.

The memorializePositions function credits the full LP balance to the NFT while the Pool only deducts the approved allowance.
By repeating minimal approvals until the Pool balance is zero, a user can exponentially inflate their NFT position to claim excessive rewards and governance power.

If the RewardsManager contract is underfunded, claims are capped by its current token balance, causing accumulated rewards to be lost.
Unclaimed rewards cannot be retrieved later, leading to permanent reward loss.

An attacker can call moveLiquidity to move funds into a bankrupted bucket, which is not validated by the contract.
This effectively revives the bucket and allows the attacker to redeem wiped-out LP shares, stealing value from other users.

Because _claimRewards does not validate isEpochClaimed, a user can repeatedly trigger it via moveStakedLiquidity to claim the same epoch’s rewards multiple times.
This enables double-claiming and drains protocol funds.
updateBucketExchangeRatesAndClaim fails to validate pool_ as a legitimate pool, allowing an attacker to supply a malicious contract and drain all reward tokens.
Because no minimum voting threshold exists, an attacker can submit a self-transfer proposal with dust votes during low activity periods to capture unallocated funds.

Delegate rewards are distributed quadratically by vote count, giving whales a disproportionate share while discouraging smaller delegates.
This undermines decentralization and reduces governance participation from less powerful voters.

_updateBucketExchangeRateAndCalculateRewards performs division before multiplication, causing precision loss and systematically underpaying user rewards.
The error grows with the amount of interest earned, making larger rewards more inaccurate.

The updateBucketExchangeRatesAndClaim function is vulnerable to MEV frontrunning, allowing bots to consistently capture update rewards.
This results in unfair reward distribution and discourages honest users from maintaining bucket states.
Calculating new rewards is susceptible to precision loss due to division before multiplication.

getPositionIndexesFiltered is compiled with Solidity 0.8.14 and hits a known optimizer bug where inline assembly memory writes may be removed.
This can corrupt the returned array length and break function correctness.

Due to snapshot inconsistencies, screeningVote and voteExtraordinary grant different voting power when called at the exact start block versus later blocks.
This allows attackers to mint or dispose tokens at the distribution start block to unfairly manipulate voting power.

In the Extraordinary Funding mechanism, thresholds depend on the live total supply, allowing attackers to burn tokens and reduce the required quorum.
This lets under-supported proposals pass and siphon treasury funds, posing a severe risk to protocol reserves.
Because proposeExtraordinary excludes endBlock from the proposal hash, an attacker can frontrun with the same parameters but a malicious expiry block.

RewardsManager unsafely casts uint256 values to uint128 when storing LP balances and exchange rates, creating overflow risk.
This can lead to incorrect reward calculations, lost rewards, or transaction failures in extreme cases.

StandardFunding.fundingVote lets users who skipped the screening stage vote in the funding stage, yet these users cannot claim rewards.
This locks a portion of rewards permanently, causing mismatches between the treasury balance and actual distributable rewards.

subtag: Does not match with Doc, Incorrect Parameter
description: The voting threshold in Extraordinary Proposals is miscalculated by treating treasury token requests as non-treasury ratios, resulting in lower-than-expected requirements. This flaw enables attackers to drain the treasury over multiple proposals without needing full non-treasury support.

PositionManager and PermitERC721 fail to comply with EIP-4494 by omitting required interfaces and functions, breaking signature tracking and compatibility. As a result, tools and contracts cannot detect ERC721 permit support, undermining usability and standard conformance.

PositionManager.moveLiquidity may underflow and revert if vars.lpbAmountFrom exceeds fromPosition.lps, which can happen due to accrued interest or price shifts. This stems from failing to clear outdated LP records post-liquidity move.
With a very large cross chain token transfer, a malicious party can use this to steal the same amount from the express receive executor.

subtag: ERC777 Callback, Violating CEI / Missing nonReentrant
description: A malicious actor can trick a TokenManager into thinking that a bigger amount of tokens were transferred.
A large token holder can send back and forth tokens using the flow limit to the capacity in the start of every epoch, making the system unusable(DOS)
when token is ERC777 token, the token receiver can manipulate its balance in order to increase flow in more than it should be
Different EVM and non-EVM chains support different address formats (e.g., case sensitivity), which may cause validateSender to fail.
InterchainProposalExecutor._execute is called from a non-payable function, and thus native coins cannot be passed in the call
the refund address is error, using msg.sender directly

After the ownership of the RemoteAddressValidator contract is transferred, the trusted addresses can no longer be modified. If the previous owner had added a malicious contract, it would still be considered valid and could deploy new token managers and tokens.
When the vote threshold is met, the onlySigners modifier resets the counter and triggers an external call. If all signers vote within the same block, it may lead to double counting.
Insufficient support for tokens with different decimal places across chains can lead to loss of funds during cross-chain bridging.

Different chains use different contract address formats, which can cause issues during cross-chain operations. Contracts may fail to interpret addresses correctly, making it impossible to whitelist addresses from certain chains. Additionally, non-EVM chains may be unable to interact with EVM-based chains.
safeTransferFrom() does not ensure that the actual number of tokens received is the same as the input amount.
Identifying publications using its ID makes the protocol vulnerable to blockchain re-orgs

tryMigrate() function does not check whether followerProfileId is already following any data. If a user calls follow() again after upgrading to V2, it may result in the same user following the same data twice, causing _followerCount to be incorrectly incremented and the state of _followDataByFollowTokenId to become inconsistent.

The contract fails to properly check user permissions, preventing users from performing intended actions. When a user attempts to follow using a wrapped followTokenId, if the user is not the owner of the corresponding follow NFT or has not been authorized, they are unable to unfollow. This means that users cannot control their own follow actions without owning the respective follow NFT.

When the system is paused, users should not be able to execute the unfollow() operation due to the whenNotPaused modifier. However, users can bypass this restriction by calling removeFollower() or burn() in the FollowNFT contract, which lack the whenNotPaused modifier, allowing them to unfollow even while the system is paused.

There is a lack of proper operation restrictions for whitelisted profile creators, allowing them to mint handles corresponding to V1 Profiles. If someone else mints the same handle after the V2 upgrade, the corresponding V1 profile will be permanently unable to be migrated using batchMigrateProfiles().

In MetaTxLib.validatePostSignature(), the postParams.actionModules array is not encoded before being passed into abi.encode. In MetaTxLib.validateChangeDelegatedExecutorsConfigSignature(), delegatedExecutors and approvals arrays are encoded using abi.encodePacked() without wrapping in keccak256. These encoding methods deviate from EIP-712 standards, causing calls to revert.
The signature verification of the typehash differs from the EIP-712 standard, causing calls to revert.

In approve(), the token guardian check is insufficient. Even if the owner has enabled the token guardian, an already authorized operator can still call the approve() function to set token allowances, meaning the owner's tokens could be controlled by an unauthorized operator.
Users cannot follow themselves on V2, but users who own a follow NFT from V1 can call FollowNFT::tryMigrate() on V2 to follow themselves.
By calling FollowNFT::tryMigrate(), a user can follow themselves without the consent of others.
Through executing batchMigrateFollows, blocked followers can continue to follow, because FollowNFT.tryMigrate does not check whether the user has been blocked.
The protocol allows ERC-777 tokens to be used as emission tokens.A liquidated user can trigger tokenReceived in ERC-777 to revert the entire liquidation.
The contract does not use Chainlink Aggregator’s minAnswer / maxAnswer to validate returned prices (most data feeds no longer use these according to Chainlink docs).

Improper verification logic for cross-chain governance messages (VAA). If the guardian set changes during the delay period, the same VAA may fail verification in executeProposal because Wormhole checks VAA validity against the current active guardian set.
The contract sends rewards for each emissionConfig’s emissionToken. If the emissionToken is malicious (e.g., reverts on transfer), the entire transaction fails.
The guardian has pause authority, but the contract does not override transferOwnership. Only the current guardian (owner) can change the guardian, preventing normal ownership transfer.

grantGuardiansPause lacks a whenNotPaused check, allowing it to execute while paused, setting guardianPauseAllowed = true and bypassing permissionlessUnpause and togglePause asserts.
The guardian can call renounceOwnership to remove themselves as owner, and the contract has no mechanism for governance to reclaim ownership.
impact: If the sequence pause → grantGuardianPause → renounceOwnership occurs, the contract cannot be unpaused via permissionlessUnpause. No one can control TemporalGovernor since the owner is address(0), and only the owner can call revokeGuardian. The contract becomes permanently paused, unable to process any proposals.

The guardian can execute cross-chain proposals while the contract is paused and does not check whether the intendedRecipient is the contract itself.
As long as the cross-chain proposal’s calldata matches the expected format, the guardian can bypass validation and execute the proposal even if intendedRecipient points to another contract.

fastTrackProposalExecution lacks the whenPaused modifier.
The owner can bypass the normal voting process and execute any proposal even when the contract is not paused, contrary to the intended “use only when paused” design.

If a proposal includes transferring native tokens to a target address, execution fails because the contract lacks a receive or payable function.
impact: The proposal reverts during execution.

During deployment, each market is initialized with a hardcoded initialMintAmount of 1e18.
For tokens with units smaller than 1e18, the deployer cannot provide such a large initial amount, causing minting (and deployment) to fail.

During deployment, an incorrect address was set as the Wormhole Core contract address. This address has no corresponding contract deployed on the Base mainnet.
impact: The TemporalGovernor contract will revert when executing parseAndVerifyVM through this address. Since the contract cannot execute proposals, the initialization tokens held internally (used to prevent immediate market attacks) cannot be transferred or utilized and become locked. Additionally, the entire TemporalGovernor contract becomes non-functional, unable to accept or execute proposals.

The chainId for Base mainnet was set incorrectly.
Deployment is invalid and requires redeployment.
Exception handling logic for deprecated markets was not implemented.Deprecated markets cannot be liquidated.

Accumulated but unclaimed rewards for suppliers and borrowers were not distributed before the admin replaced the reward distribution contract.
Once the replacement occurs, users' previously accumulated rewards may become permanently unclaimable.

When executing lending operations, the current borrowRateMantissa is calculated based on the utilizationRate. If this interest rate exceeds borrowRateMaxMantissa, the contract will forcibly revert.
impact: If reserves > cash, it will cause utilizationRate > 1, making borrowRateMantissa > borrowRateMaxMantissa and triggering a revert. User funds become locked and cannot be withdrawn or used to repay debts.

When the contract sets reward tokens for different mTokens, it restricts the reward speed to not exceed 100 * 1e18.
Different reward tokens have different decimals, making it impossible to fairly limit the reward speed (< 18 → reward distribution limit is greater than expected; > 18 → reward distribution becomes nearly impossible to execute).

subtag: Does not match with Doc, Incorrect Parameter
description:
The borrowRateMaxMantissa setting was not adjusted for specific chains.
On chains with shorter block times, extremely high annualized borrowing interest rates are allowed.

castVoteWithReasonAndParamsBySig allows others to vote on behalf of a user via signature, but the signed data does not include a nonce. An attacker can reuse the same signature multiple times, concentrating a user’s votes on a specific candidate and manipulating election results.

The relay allows the contract owner to modify fullWeightDuration or votingPeriod without checking for ongoing proposals, enabling election parameters to be changed mid-vote.The contract owner can influence voting outcomes—for example, increasing fullWeightDuration so that late voters gain disproportionately higher weight.

When calculating the next election date, firstNominationStartDate.day is used directly without accounting for differences in the number of days between months.
 The election interval can be extended to more than six months.
GovernorUpgradeable & EIP712Upgradeable contracts remain uninitialized.

Lack of a tracking mechanism for removed members, and the authority to add new members is entirely controlled by the Security Council. A member can be re-added within the same lifecycle even after being voted out by the DAO.

subtag: Implementation Error, Invalid Validation, State Update Inconsistency
description: SecurityCouncilManager, when replacing cohort members, deletes the old cohort and adds new members without checking for ongoing elections, allowing the same member to exist simultaneously in both the old and new cohort.During elections, a member might be elected to the new cohort while still part of the old cohort, causing governance confusion and disrupting the democratic process.

The lack of chain ID verification and final owner protection allows the removeOwnerAtIndex call to be replayed and executed on different chains, mistakenly removing different owners at the specified index, and even potentially removing the only owner.

During the validation process of MagicSpend.validatePaymasterUserOp(), only a single withdrawAmount check against the contract’s balance is performed. However, when multiple UserOps are batched in EntryPoint, the single-balance check cannot ensure that the total requested funds do not exceed the contract balance. When EntryPoint executes multiple UserOps() in a batch, if the total requested funds exceed the MagicSpend contract balance, subsequent postOp() executions will fail due to insufficient funds, leading to transaction reverts.

MagicSpend.validatePaymasterUserOp() and MagicSpend.withdraw()  use the same signature. Malicious users can submit a transaction via the paymaster and then front-run with a withdraw() call, causing validatePaymasterUserOp() to revert because the nonce has already been consumed.
The V3Vault does not check the token address in the permit2 signature, allowing attackers to withdraw USDC from the vault using any ERC20 approval.
onERC721Received calls _cleanupLoan to perform external NFT transfers before completing core state updates, violating the CEI pattern.
The transform() function of V3Vault does not verify the ownership of the tokenId in the data parameter, allowing attackers to manipulate and tamper with the NFT positions of other depositors.
V3Utils.execute() lacks caller verification, allowing anyone with authorization to steal the entire liquidity of another person's Uniswap V3 NFT position.
If tickCumulatives[1] - tickCumulatives[0] is negative and ((tickCumulatives[1] - tickCumulatives[0]) % twapSeconds) does not equal zero, then the returned tick will be larger than its correct value.
Malicious holders can exploit the onERC721Received callback by returning an invalid value, leading to a revert.

_updateAndCheckCollateral() only checks collateral limits during borrowing, allowing attackers to bypass the checks and exceed the collateral limits set by the protocol through the process of 'deposit → borrow → immediately withdraw.

Attackers can trigger a malicious onERC721Received callback to consume gas during the AutoRange::execute()process, forcing a revert and leading to continuous consumption of protocol fees and a DoS scenario for the contract.
The protocol lacks minLoanSize check.There will be no incentive for liquidators to liquidate small underwater positions given the gas cost.

Due to interest updates occurring only once per block, borrowers can take and repay loans within the same block without accruing interest, enabling arbitrage and low-cost DoS attacks that block other users from borrowing.

V3Vault’s setReserveFactor updates the reserve factor without first updating global interest rates, causing the new reserve factor to retroactively affect lending rates and potentially create unexpected or unfair borrow/supply rates.

Due to an off-by-one-style miscalculation in _resetDailyLendIncreaseLimit and _resetDailyDebtIncreaseLimit, users can deposit or borrow up to ~110% of allowed daily limits instead of being correctly constrained, effectively bypassing the protocol’s daily asset limits.
When referenceTokenDecimals is 18 chainlinkPriceX96 is higher than some threshold between 18 and 19 (in Q96 notation), it will cause arithmetic overflow.

dailyLendIncreaseLimitLeft and dailyDebtIncreaseLimitLeft are not correctly adjusted when _withdraw or _repayare called before a deposit/borrow in the same day, causing the protocol to incorrectly enforce daily limits and allowing users to bypass intended daily restrictions.
Liquidation rewards are sent to msg.sender instead of the intended recipient specified in LiquidateParams, breaking composability and potentially redirecting incentives.
When an AutoCompoundVault is deactivated, users’ tokens can become stuck because withdrawLeftoverBalances relies on the vault being active to determine ownership.
_checkLoanIsHealthy lacks a safety buffer, allowing borrowers at the maximum loan limit to be unfairly liquidated due to minor market fluctuations.
_deposit checks totalSupply() instead of converting to assets, allowing users to exceed the global lending limit.

The execute() uses the old configuration from positionConfigs[tokenId] without verifying that the configuration was set by the current NFT owner, potentially allowing users to execute the token settings of the previous owner.
V3Vault is not ERC-4626 compliant
Anyone can call a repayment operation with a value of 0, leading to the incorrect removal of newly created user positions and resulting in asset loss.

subtag: Liquidation - Dust repay / front run evade liquidation
description: Both repay and liquidate calls will fail if the amount of shares that the transaction attempts to repay exceeds the outstanding debt shares of the position, with RepayExceedsDebt and DebtChanged errors respectively.

In onlyFees mode, feeAmount should be calculated based solely on the fees, but it actually includes liquidity assets withdrawn from a previous decreaseLiquidity() call. This results in an overestimation of reward calculations, causing holders to pay more rewards than expected.

subtag: Bad Condition, Price Manipulation / Arbitrage opportunity, Unfair Liquidation
description: The TWAP verification logic in AutoRange and AutoExit is overly strict, resulting in a scenario where users are unable to exit their positions for stop-loss purposes even if they opt not to perform a swap. This forces assets to be locked during periods of high market volatility.
V3Oracle uses the manipulable spot price to derive the number of position tokens, meaning that even if the price is verified by the oracle, the valuation calculation can still be distorted.

When the admin sets the collateralFactor of a token to 0 to remove its collateral eligibility, the liquidation process will have collateralValue calculated as 0. This ultimately leads to the liquidation logic reverting due to division by 0, rendering the associated loans permanently unliquidatable.
Dangerous use of deadline parameter

subtag: Does not match with Doc, State Update Inconsistency
description: liquidate() does not update dailyDebtIncreaseLimitLeft after repaying the debt (liquidation), which prevents the re-borrowing data from being released. Over time, this accumulation can lead to a decrease in vault utilization and inconsistency with the logic of repay().

Users can front-run the operator's transaction execution by altering the onlyFees , changing the fee model from being based on the entire position to being calculated solely on fees. This reduces the fee percentage that the protocol can charge, resulting in a loss of revenue for the protocol.

_calculateLiquidation() calculates the liquidator's income as 10% of the fullValue instead of 10% of the debt during underwater liquidations. This leads to insufficient liquidation incentives when assets are below the debt, undermining the fair liquidation mechanism designed by the protocol.

The priceX96 is obtained by calling _getReferencePoolPriceX96(pool, 0); which returns slot zero price, while the derivedPoolPriceX96 is the price to be verified.

The problem is when priceX96 < verifyPriceX96, the difference in % is obtained by dividing the difference by verifyPriceX96 which will return a lower value
Instance

The same vault can be added to both the general and Kerosene lists, causing its collateral value to be double-counted, which inflates the collateral ratio and enables borrowers to take on excessive debt.

Partial liquidations cannot be performed and prevents liquidators from liquidating DYAD minted by whales that hold huge positions in the system. Since the liquidations cannot be performed unless the liquidator can match up to the collateral deposited and DYAD minted by the whale, the system will be undercollaterized causing bad debt to accrue.
Attacker can frontrun a deposit request with amount 0 to block the withdraw reqeust
An attacker can grief any token ID by depositing a dust amount in the same block, triggering the DepositedInSameBlock check and causing a denial-of-service on withdrawals.
Users’ funds deposited into the unbounded Kerosene vault become permanently locked due to missing decimals() support, preventing withdrawals.
Withdraw checks wrongly apply to Kerosene assets, causing deposited Kerosene to become permanently locked and unwithdrawable.
Liquidation reverts when non-kerosene collateral is insufficient, due to missing exogenous collateral checks in VaultManagerV2::liquidate.
Kerosene deposits are stuck in the unbounded vault due to assetPrice underflow when TVL is less than total DYAD supply.
Kerosene collateral is not transferred to the liquidator during full liquidation, causing the liquidator to incur a loss.
Users can bypass the system's flashloan protection by self-liquidating and moving collateral within the same block, enabling repeated exploitation without immediate detection.
The liquidation bonus is miscalculated, causing liquidators to receive insufficient collateral, weakening liquidation incentives and increasing system risk.
If cr drops below 1e18, no one will have incentive to liquidate others.
setUnboundedKerosineVault was never called during deployment, causing the bounded vault to inevitably revert when attempting to query the value of kerosene
When this borrow position is at risk of liquidation due to insufficient collateral, the kerosene liquidated will be bought at two fold the normal price.
No incentive to liquidate small positions could result in protocol going underwater

Anyone can front-run a transaction to deposit a small amount of assets into the dNFT position, thereby preventing the dNFT owner from removing a specific vault. The reason is that both remove() and removeKerosene() check:if (Vault(vault).id2asset(id) > 0) revert VaultHasAssets();As long as there are assets in the vault, the removal will fail. Attackers can observe transactions in the mempool and deposit 'dust' assets in advance, causing the victim's removal operation to revert.
VaultManagerV2.sol::burnDyad function is missing an isDNftOwner modifier, allowing a user to burn another user’s minted DYAD

addKerosine() is intended to add BoundedKerosineVault and UnboundedKerosineVault to the VaultManagerV2. But since the addKerosine() check if the vault isLicensed in KerosineManager it will always revert for kerosine vaults, because in KerosineManager are stored only the exogenous vaults based on which the kerosine price is determined.

The price of kerosene tokens can be manipulated instantaneously, leading to forced liquidation. The getKeroseneValue()function relies on the real-time price of the kerosene vault, which can change abruptly with user actions (depositing or withdrawing collateral). Attackers can exploit this to force other users into liquidation.
Insufficient balance prevents bridging, leading to a DoS attack on the bridge.

Anyone can send a "remote deployment request" to the origin chain, forcibly initializing that chain's token balance in ITSHub to zero. This can cause an underflow during cross-chain transfers, effectively preventing the origin chain from bridging tokens to other chains.

Axelar's cross-chain bridge does not properly handle rebasing tokens. This is because the system records a static token amount at the time of locking, while the actual token balance may change due to rebasing.
• In the case of a positive rebase (balance increases), the user may receive fewer tokens than they are entitled to, resulting in a loss for the user.
• In the case of a negative rebase (balance decreases), the system may attempt to transfer more tokens than it actually holds, causing the transaction to revert and funds to become stuck (DoS).
Due to the lack of restrictions preventing tokens and token managers from being deployed only on the origin chain, it becomes possible to gain control over transfers on other chains.

subtag: Incorrect Parameter, Missing Upper/Lower Bound Check
description: The denominator in the share calculation formula uses totalTokenBalanceStakers() (which can be manipulated by external transfers) instead of the actual effective staked assets. This allows attackers to manipulate the denominator with incorrect parameters, causing other users' shares to be calculated as 0, thereby enabling them to steal all assets.

When interacting with UMA, the escalate() function passes BOND as the bond parameter to UMA, leading to UMA burning an additional amount based on bond/2 and charging a finalFee. This is inconsistent with the documentation specification of "full refund of the pledge," ultimately resulting in higher costs for the protocol agents than expected.

In arbRestake, when redeeming arbRewardShares, it only decreases the overall stakeShares of the NFT but does not synchronize the reduction of the addressShares for the nftOwner. This leads to tokenBalanceOfAddress permanently reporting an inflated balance and accumulating errors.

In updateYieldStrategy(), the use of try/catch for withdrawAll() of the original strategy is incorrectly handled by unconditionally ignoring any errors. This prevents the owner from choosing to abort the switch if the withdrawal fails.
Reallocation depends on the slot0 price, which can be manipulated.

The liquidation process only checks for negative margin when the position is completely closed. This enables liquidators to bypass the compensation mechanism by leaving a very small residual position, thereby shifting the loss to the protocol.

The reallocate() function lacks verification of liquidity ownership in scenarios involving multiple trading pairs within the same range tick, leading to incorrect transfer of liquidity between other trading pairs and disrupting internal fund accounting.

During complete liquidation, the transfer source address for bad debt compensation incorrectly uses msg.sender (the market address) instead of the liquidator's address, preventing the bad debt vault from being liquidated and causing the bad debt to continue to increase.
The trading price calculation relies on Uniswap's spot prices and does not take the TWAP into account, making it vulnerable to flash loan manipulation that can affect the final transaction outcome.

updateIRMParams() and updateFeeRatio() do not settle interest rates/fees for the current cycle before updating parameters, leading to the entire period being calculated with the new parameters, which undermines the accuracy of interest rate and fee calculations.
The callUniswapObserve function does not implement downward rounding when handling negative tickCumulative values, resulting in a TWAP tick calculation that is too high and affecting price accuracy.
The PriceFeed omits checks for both staleness and round completeness in the prices returned by Chainlink, which may cause the entire protocol to use outdated or incomplete price data.

DOS attack is possible when, a malicious user creates many very small positions, which could cause excessive gas consumed and even transactions reverted when other users are trying to liquidate any of the user’s positions.
Vaults can become immune from liquidation by setting vault.recipient to a blacklisted quote token address

In reallocate(), the excess quoteToken should be returned to the redistributor, but the implementation incorrectly sets the recipient to msg.sender (the market contract), resulting in misallocated funds and losses for the redistributor.
The PriceFeed incorrectly handles the decimal differences between price pairs, leading to distorted quotes for some trading pairs and affecting asset risk calculations.

LlamaRelativeQuorum calculates the required votes for approval and disapproval when creating governance proposals by setting actionApprovalSupply / actionDisapprovalSupply to the number of role holders (getRoleSupplyAsNumberOfHolders()). However, when calculating the actual number of approved votes, it uses the quantity of each holder instead of a fixed 1 vote per holder. This results in members holding multiple tokens having an overly disproportionate influence, allowing them to prematurely meet the quorum conditions.

LlamaRelativeQuorum.validateActionCreation() is defined as external and does not include any authorization checks, allowing anyone to re-invoke it after an action has been created to overwrite the snapshot values of actionApprovalSupply and actionDisapprovalSupply.

LlamaCore.executeAction() supports governance actions with msg.value, but it does not pass that value down when calling LlamaExecutor.execute(), and LlamaExecutor.execute() is also not marked as payable.

castDisapproval() only checks if the proposal is in the "queued" state in _preCastAssertions() and does not simultaneously check block.timestamp < minExecutionTime. This allows a proposal to be voted against even when it has reached the executable time, causing the proposal to immediately transition to a rejected state and resulting in a failed execution.
A user can create 24 * 3600 * 30 ~ 2.5 mils actions to DOS a system in a month

The _syncVotingPower() function is missing a lower bound check when reducing voting power, failing to verify whether the subtraction exceeds the existing voting power. This can lead to integer underflow during the subtraction, causing the transaction to revert.

The voting power calculation lacks time-weighted or holding period validation, relying solely on a single block balance snapshot for verification. This allows the governance system to be manipulated by short-term borrowing or sudden positions.

The queryVotePower() function uses the state-modifying and high-cost findAndClear() in the kick-out process, lacking a low-cost logic for merely querying. This allows attackers to exhaust gas by processing large amounts of historical records, preventing the removal of GSC members.

The NFTBoostVault lacks a mechanism to automatically synchronize the voting power of all relevant accounts after the multiplier is updated, and it does not compute the multiplier voting power based on the block at which the proposal is created during voting. This can result in votes being erroneously calculated based on outdated multipliers.
Admin is allowed to update merkleRoot. But some users won't be able to claim correct amount because of inconsistent check in claiming function.
gscApprove can overwrite the approved allowance of the same spender from previously approved value

The day in blocks is calculated with the block time as 13.3 seconds in CoreVoting.sol.: uint256 public constant DAY_IN_BLOCKS = 6496;, but since moving to proof of stake, block times are fixed to 12 seconds per blockThis results in an incorrect calculation of the lockDuration and extraVoteTime, which is used in setting the total duration of a proposal should be active and also the max vote time.

The gscApprove() function, when adjusting the spender allowance, only subtracts the new amount from gscAllowance, lacking logic to synchronize the return of the remaining balance when reducing the allowance. This results in inconsistencies between gscAllowance and the ERC20 allowance status, making it impossible to lower the limit.
The incorrect restriction of msg.sender to axelarGateway results in legitimate cross-chain messages being unable to pass, leading to a DoS.

The authorization message is not bound to a specific liquidity pool, allowing signatures to be reused in other pools with the same batch tokens, enabling malicious trades to front-run and consume the authorization.

The contract caches the DOMAIN_SEPARATOR in the constructor without initializing name, resulting in the computed domain separator being inconsistent with the standard EIP-2612 requirements, causing the permit signature to fail verification.

The deposit and mint functions do not verify the relationship between the recipient and the caller, as well as the origin of the assets. This allows an attacker to inject small amounts of funds into another user's account, disrupting subsequent transactions and causing a denial of service (DoS).

Due to the use of average calculations and rounding errors in calculateDepositPrice across multiple requests with different prices, _trancheTokenAmount may exceed maxMint, causing some investors to prematurely overclaim their shares. This results in subsequent users experiencing transaction failures due to insufficient quantities when claiming assets.

DelayedAdmin does not store the address of PauseAdmin and lacks a method to call removePauser, resulting in the failure of the emergency removal process for pausers as designed in the documentation, undermining the expected security model.

The _calculateTrancheTokenAmount function in processWithdraw and previewWithdraw consistently uses rounding down, which violates the best practices of EIP-4626 that require rounding up for withdrawals. This may result in users consuming fewer shares than they should, leading to asset losses for the vault or incorrect calculations of remaining limits.

RestrictionManager.detectTransferRestriction only checks whether the recipient address is a valid member and does not verify whether the sender's address is on the blacklist. This allows restricted accounts to freely transfer tokens, circumventing the trading restriction rules designed by the contract.

The final check in deltaHedgeAmount lacks validation of the sign for tokensToSwap, resulting in negative amounts being incorrectly reversed to positive numbers when close to the position. This erroneous hedging direction can be maliciously exploited to manipulate the vault's positions.

The volatility model directly combines the utilization of bull and bear market options without distinguishing between directional and premium difference conditions. This allows low-priced options trades to impact the pricing of high-priced options, creating opportunities for arbitrage.
Malicious users can exploit the new Smilee vault by using donations to execute a classic first depositor/ERC4626 inflation attack.
Incorrect strike parameters were stored, causing subsequent burns to be unable to locate the position and permanently locking it.
Whenever swapPrice > oraclePrice, minting via PositionManager will revert, due to not enough funds being obtained from user.

LP can transfer their shares to another LP through ERC20 transfer. Thus, when the second LP withdraws these shares, they will not be deducted from _state.liquidity.totalDeposit. This way, _state.liquidity.totalDeposit will not reflect the actual amount of deposits, leading to various issues.

The safeTransferFrom function attempts to send funds from itself, which requires the contract to first approve itself to increase its allowance. However, there is no self-approval logic in the contract. As a result, this refund functionality fails every time. Instead, safeTransfer() should be used for refunds.

The FeeManager.trackVaultFee and receiveFee functions lack authorization checks, allowing any contract to impersonate the vault or DVP identity and arbitrarily increase fee records. This compromises accounting data and can lead to DVP operation rollbacks.

The delta calculation formula for out-of-the-money options directly returns 0, ignoring their actual price sensitivity. This leads to the vault not hedging the risks associated with such positions, violating the principle that 'traders' profits should not translate into LP losses.

The deltaHedgeAmount function uses the comparison condition sideTokensAmount/10000 to determine whether small amounts of side tokens are allowed for sale. For cases where the balance is 0 or extremely low, this condition will always fail, causing almost all IG short trades to revert under such circumstances.

In multiple functions, safeApprove() is used to set another non-zero value directly from a non-zero allowance without first setting the allowance to 0, triggering the protection checks in OpenZeppelin's SafeERC20. This results in subsequent mint/burn/sell processes being reverted.

In PortfolioToken.sol:_fromVirtualAfterTotalChangedForMint() the integer division div(mul(virtualAmount, realTotal), totalVirtual) causes rounding down to zero when realTotal is minimal and totalVirtual is inflated through donations, combined with automatic donation processing in _subDepositRewardsPoolCheck() that treats any contract token balance as legitimate rewards.

subtag: Invalid Slippage Control / Missing slippage check
description: The deposit function lacks a slippage check mechanism, which results in users minting at unfavorable ratios when the liquidity pool is unbalanced, leading to potential losses.
PoolOracle utilizes vulnerable OZ 4.3.1 UUPS implementation

The swapCallback function verifies msg.sender solely based on the result of _getPool(), without confirming whether the address corresponds to a valid pool deployed by the factory. This creates an opportunity for address collisions that can bypass the check and exhaust quota resources.

SignatureQueue.validateOrder checks signatures using Consensus.checkSignatures.
But this doesn't check duplication of signers, so malicious attacker can bypass threshold checking.

The RedeemQueue batches exclude shares when processing critical timestamps, while the eligibility check still allows claims for that timestamp. This leads to inconsistencies between batch records and claim eligibility, resulting in the premature consumption of shares by legitimate users.

The balance inquiry logic between the vault and the redemption hooks lacks handling for native tokens. By uniformly using ERC20 balanceOf, the native token withdrawal functionality becomes ineffective.

Because during batch processing of multi-asset reports only the base asset’s timestamp is updated, protocol fees are repeatedly calculated and accumulated within the same time period, resulting in excessive fees.

The performance fee calculation formula incorrectly multiplies the price difference by the total number of shares, failing to accurately convert the fee amount based on the per-share price, resulting in calculation discrepancies.
The flaws in the redemption logic design result in shares not being accounted for in fees during the processing wait time, allowing users to circumvent the intended charging mechanism.

subtag: Bad Condition, Does not match with Doc
description: The whitelist checking logic in the updateChecks function contradicts the documentation, resulting in accounts marked as transferable being blocked instead.
ETH redemptions via SignatureRedeemQueue are broken due to missing receive function

When recording deposited stETH amounts, the contract fails to account for the downward rounding error inherent in share-based transfers, causing the internal accounting balance to exceed the actual balance. As a result, subsequent transfers fail due to insufficient funds.

The protocol fee calculation in ShareModule.handleReport function suffers from exponential compounding instead of linear accumulation. When handleReport is called frequently (e.g., daily), the protocol fee is applied to the current total shares which includes all previously accrued fees, leading to higher-than-intended fee extraction.

The cancelDepositRequest() function incorrectly uses the price checkpoint index as the deposit queue index for modification, leading to an out-of-bounds index and a revert, preventing users from canceling pending deposits.

The TokenizedShareManager._update() function only mints and locks new shares after completing the first lockup check, allowing users to immediately transfer shares that should have been locked in the same transaction, thereby circumventing the targeted lockup mechanism.

The system lacks asset allowance checks when summarizing and extracting assets from sub-treasuries, leading to a situation where the presence of a sub-treasury holding a non-zero balance of unsupported assets triggers a revert and interrupts the redemption process.

The protocol mints fee shares to the feeRecipient during deposits, redemptions, and protocol fee collection. However, the ShareManager.mint() function applies the targetLockup to all recipients, including the feeRecipient. Since this lock resets on every mint, a malicious user can repeatedly trigger minting operation and redeeming minimal amounts to continually reset the lock timer. As a result, the feeRecipient's shares remain perpetually locked and unusable, leading to a DOS where protocol fees become inaccessible.
The contract does not handle stETH rebase rewards during the waiting period in the deposit queue, resulting in excess assets being stuck in the queue.
Design intended to add only the new shortfall to the existing shortfall, but implementation added the existing shortfall twice, causing double-counting.

withdrawTo checks collateral margin using maintenanceInvariant without first syncing the oracle price, allowing margin checks to pass based on outdated price data and enabling withdrawals from undercollateralized positions.
Collateral contract does not verify that a given product address was deployed by the factory, allowing attackers to register malicious products that bypass margin requirements and steal collateral.
The Collateral.initialize function lacks an initializer check, allowing multiple initializations and enabling attackers to run malicious setup before the legitimate factory configuration.
Chainlink’s latestRoundData might return stale or incorrect results
When encountering a non-existent token config, it will always return the token config of the first index (index 0) which is a valid token config for a completely different token.
Incorrectly using uint(-1) as a non-existent comparison value.

The rewards per market are proportional to their totalBorrows which can be changed by a large holder who deposits lots of collateral, takes out a huge borrow in the market, updates the rewards, and then unwinds the position.

The Create contract fails to validate extra ERC20 tokens (tips) added to Seaport order fulfillment. Attackers can append a malicious ERC20 token that always reverts on transfer, causing the rented asset to be permanently locked inside the rental safe.

The gnosis guard doesn't have any validation or checks for the address parameter of the function setFallbackHandler(address handler), which is the function used by the rental safe owner to set a fallback handler his safe.

reNFT does not register the rental except after swapping the tokens, in addition to safeTransferFrom() being used to transfer ERC1155 tokens, which would of course, trigger the callback function onERC1155Receive() on the borrower's safe.
The gnosis_safe_disable_module_offset constant was incorrectly specified to point at an incorrect function parameter of the disableModule(address prevModule, address module).
Specifically, the offset constant will point at the prevModule (1st param) instead of the module (2nd param).

The EIP-712 RentalOrder hash derivation does not include the rentalWallet field, enabling attackers to reuse or spoof valid order hashes. The stopRent validation logic is insufficiently strict, allowing any user matching the lender field to stop an order without verifying whether it actually exists or was fulfilled properly.
The attacker exploits SeaPort's skip-on-same-address logic to create fake rentals that update escrow balances without real transfers, enabling ERC20 theft upon rent termination.
An attacker can exploit partial fills to reuse the same order hash, causing only part of the lender’s assets to be released, while the rest remain locked and unstoppably rented.

A malicious lender can indefinitely freeze a borrower’s ERC1155 tokens by preventing rental finalization, exploiting the guard's inability to distinguish rented vs. non-rented tokens of the same tokenId.
A malicious borrower can exploit the permit() function in ERC-721 tokens to self-authorize transfers and steal rented NFTs from the rental safe.
Large rental orders can exceed the block gas limit when calling stopRent(), making them impossible to stop and permanently locking assets in the protocol.
Disabling the onStop hook after rental creation causes stopRent() to revert, resulting in a DoS condition where assets and funds remain locked indefinitely.
If an ERC777 token is used for payment, a malicious renter can revert in the tokensReceived() hook during stopRent(), causing a DoS where the lender's assets remain permanently locked.

Guard.sol fails to block burn, burnFrom, and permit calls, allowing a renter to destroy or hijack rented NFTs and bypass protocol safeguards.
The Guard::checkTransaction enforces a 4-byte minimum data length, blocking native ETH transfers with empty calldata, and causing ETH to be permanently stuck in safes.
After a guard policy upgrade, rental safes can continue using outdated Guard.sol, bypassing new restrictions and compromising security enforcement.
It fails to hash dynamic types like bytes using keccak256, mistakenly uses abi.encode instead of abi.encodePacked, and omits required fields in struct hashing.
Guard.sol does not account for burnable & pausable tokens (which are quite common as well). This means lenders could lose such assets if the renter acts maliciously.

In the function validateOrder there is no way to verify whether the signature from backend signer is being reused / more importantly no way to verify that this signature was signed to rent out this particular order.
A malicious lender can make the NFT return fail via safeTransferFrom reverts, blocking stopRent() and griefing the renter out of their payment.

The blacklist mechanism does not check restrictions within the transaction process, only applying to the current balance. This allows sanctioned accounts to bypass the limitations and continue trading.

PREDICATE_ADDRESS is hardcoded to a fixed ERC20Predicate address, preventing dynamic retrieval of the correct predicate based on tokenType or external changes. This results in an inability to bridge tokens from different predicates, lacking adaptability.

The protocol uses Pyth's getPriceUnsafe() to obtain prices and only checks if the value is greater than 0, lacking an expiry check. This allows outdated and potentially manipulatable prices to enter the liquidation logic, resulting in financial losses for borrowers.

_calculateMaxBorrowCollateral subtracts unutilizedLeveragePercentage when calculating the maximum borrow collateral limit, causing an underflow and revert, which prevents the repay function from executing and subsequently triggers token liquidation.
